:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf{i} + x^2\,\mathbf{j}$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $9x^2 + y^2 = 9.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{1^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{3^2} = 1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} +3\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos t, \qquad
y = 3\sin t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =xy=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{2}={cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\cos t, \textrm d u = -\sin t\,\textrm d t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }9\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }10\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{1}^{1}10{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i+5\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $25{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $5,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for cosine, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(5)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5{cos}^{2}⁡t+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={5(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{4}+\frac{1}{2}t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =5(0+\pi -1)-5(0-1) \\  & =5\pi \end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{2}\,i+xy\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $4{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=36.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $3$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =xy=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+18{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }26{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1}26{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3x=12\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =3y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24{cos}^{2}⁡t+24{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24\,\text{d}t \\  & =24t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =24(2\pi -0) \\  & =48\pi \end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $1,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x-16y=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =x+y=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4{cos}^{2}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\,\text{d}t \\  & =4t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =4(2\pi -0) \\  & =8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=7\,i+2\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36.$

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $6.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =7, \\ Q(x,y) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(7)\cdot (6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(2)\cdot (-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }42\operatorname{cos}⁡t+12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(42\operatorname{sin}⁡t-12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(0-12)-(0-12) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{3}\,i+{x}^{3}\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={1}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{3}={sin}^{3}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{3}={cos}^{3}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({cos}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({sin}^{2}+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(y-x)\,i-(x+y)\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={3}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y-x=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-(x+y)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-9(2\pi -0) \\  & =-18\pi \end{aligned}
$$

\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $3$ and $4,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1-x=1-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =x-y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(1-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-12{cos}^{2}⁡t+9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-12{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t+9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t-12{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t+9{\int }_{0}^{0}u\,\text{d}u-12{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0-12t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =4(0-0)-12(2\pi -0) \\  & =-24\pi \end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=8\,i-(x+3)\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={2}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $2.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =8, \\ Q(x,y) & =x+3=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for sine, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(8)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(16\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i-5\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={5}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $5.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for cosine, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-5)\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }25{cos}^{2}⁡t-25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =25{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1}{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =25(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{4}+\frac{1}{2}t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =25(0+\pi +1)-(0+1) \\  & =25\pi \end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $4{x}^{2}+25{y}^{2}=100.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $5$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={e}^{y}={e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}, \\ Q(x,y) & ={e}^{x}={e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitutions $u=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,du=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt$ and $v=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,dv=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u+{\int }_{1}^{1}{e}^{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$
